newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine National Bank hopes for better times.
newsitem.headline: Philippine National Bank hopes for better times.

text.p: The Philippine National Bank (PNB) on Thursday reported a sharp decline in its 1996 net income, but officials said it aimed to regain its stature as an industry leader.

The bank registered a 17 percent drop in core income to 1.708 billion pesos ($64 million) in 1996 from 2.058 billion ($78 million) the previous year. Inclusive of non-recurring items, which are mostly from the sale of assets, the bank's net income reached 4.675 billion pesos ($177 million).
The bank had earlier downgraded its full-year target to 1.7 billion pesos from 2.0 billion pesos ($75 million) after it posted disappointing nine-month results.

"With a big transformation this year...We're looking at a 25 to 30 percent growth on the regular income as a very conservative target for this year," PNB senior executive vice president Valentin Araneta told analysts.
He said the bank's loan portfolio, which grew by 38 percent to 97.1 billion pesos ($3.685 billion) last year, would be able to sustain a 25 to 30 percent expansion in coming years.
"1997 and 1998 will be catch-up years for us. We'll be able to catch up with the big banks," PNB president Peter Favila later told Reuters.

He said PNB hoped to join the ranks of its former peers Bank of the Philippine, Philippine Commercial International Bank PS, Far East Bank and Trust Co Inc and Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co Inc as the bank's corporate restructuring was completed.

"We are converting the bank from a mere service organisation to a full marketing company as we put to advantage the bank's 80 years of banking relationship, our geographical presence of 304 domestic branches and 69 overseas offices," Favila told analysts.

"We see harder work ahead of us as we continue to bring the whole organisation, in the fastest manner possible, out of transition in the midst of thinning margins, threats to market shares and very innovative bank products and services," he added.
But analyst were less sanguine about the bank's prospects.
Audi Pantillano, analyst at Angping Securities, said it would be hard for PNB to attain its target due to the thinning margins and its bloated workforce.
He said the bank's cheap source of funds, such as government deposits, was slowly being taken away by state-owned banks.
Last year, PNB cuts its workforce to 7,730 from 8,100 and more jobs are expected to be cut. Favila declined to say how many workers would be affected.
PNB, which used to be controlled by the Philippine government, started slipping from its top position in the early 1990s.

PNB was partially privatised in December 1995 and recently received a boost to its capital when majority private shareholders approved an increase in capital to 25 billion pesos from the previous 10 billion pesos.
The government now holds 49.8 percent of the bank.
